title: Archive access
brief: Develop a service design proposal for a small local-history archive moving from ad hoc walk-ins to a reservable study room. One staff member, two desks, a shared magnifier, no public Wi-Fi. Researchers include school groups, family historians and people who cannot use online forms. Twenty percent of requests arrive without a catalog reference. Staff cannot promise that an item is usable until its condition has been checked. A 10-week pilot can use paper, telephone and the existing web form; no new software procurement. Give the director and front-desk team enough detail to pilot it, including a difficult user journey and what they should learn.

# Reservable Study Room: Service Design Proposal for a 10-Week Pilot

## Summary

The archive should replace ad hoc walk-ins with bookable desk sessions, run from one paper diary at the front desk. The pilot rests on four rules:

1. **The diary is the only record of bookings.** Telephone calls, web form submissions and in-person requests are all written into it by staff. The web form requests a booking; it never confirms one.
2. **Confirmation happens in two steps.** The desk is confirmed first. Items are confirmed only after their condition has been checked.
3. **A catalog reference is not required.** Researchers who cannot name an item get a short, structured conversation and a bounded search.
4. **Nobody leaves without a next step.** Walk-ins are seated if a desk is free, or booked on the spot if not.

The pilot needs no new software. It needs a diary, a one-page request slip, a tally sheet and a protected block of staff time for preparation.

## Decisions needed from the director before week 1

- **Opening pattern.** This proposal assumes three public days a week and one half-day closed for preparation. The session structure works with other patterns, but the preparation half-day is essential.
- **Group size.** Set the maximum school group the room can safely hold.
- **Photography.** Decide whether researchers may photograph items with their own phones, since there is no Wi-Fi and many will ask.
- **Closure cover.** Agree what happens when the one staff member is absent (proposed below).

## How the service works

### Sessions and capacity

Each public day has two sessions: 10:00–12:30 and 1:30–4:00. Each session offers two desks, so a three-day week provides 12 desk-sessions. One session a week is reserved for groups and uses both desks, leaving 10 individual desk-sessions and one group session.

| Time | Staff activity |
|---|---|
| 9:00–10:00 | Telephone line staffed; items set out for the day |
| 10:00–12:30 | Morning session; answerphone on |
| 12:30–1:30 | Room closed; morning items returned |
| 1:30–4:00 | Afternoon session; answerphone on |
| 4:00–5:00 | Items returned; call-backs; web form requests entered in the diary |

The preparation half-day is used for retrieval, condition checks, searches for requests without references, and confirmation calls.

### Making a request

Researchers can ask in three ways, and all three are treated equally:

- **Telephone.** The line is staffed 9:00–10:00 on public days. At other times the answerphone promises a call back within two working days.
- **Web form.** The existing form is unchanged except for one added sentence: "This is a request. We will telephone or email to confirm your desk."
- **In person.** Front-desk staff complete the request slip with the researcher.

Requests must arrive at least five working days before the visit, and each researcher may ask for up to five items per session. Both limits protect the preparation time and should be tested in the pilot.

### The request slip

There is one slip per visit, kept in the diary at the session page. It records:

- name and preferred contact method, including the best time to telephone;
- session booked and desk (A or B);
- items requested, by reference or by description;
- whether the magnifier is needed;
- any access needs, such as seating, large-print finding aids or a companion;
- the condition outcome for each item and the date the researcher was told.

### Two-step confirmation

**Step 1: desk confirmed.** At the first contact, staff offer a session and say: "Your desk is booked. We will check the condition of the items and telephone you by [date] to tell you what you will be able to see."

**Step 2: items confirmed.** On the preparation half-day, each item is checked and given one of three outcomes.

| Outcome | Meaning | What the researcher is told |
|---|---|---|
| Ready | Can be used at the desk | "It will be waiting for you." |
| Restricted | Usable with conditions, such as staff turning the pages or a copy instead | The condition, and whether it changes what they can do |
| Not available | Too fragile to produce | Why, and what else is offered: a copy, a related item or a later date |

The researcher is told at least two working days before the visit. If every item is not available, they choose whether to come anyway, change the request or release the desk.

### Requests without a catalog reference

About one request in five will arrive as a description. Staff use five prompts:

- Who or what is it about?
- Where?
- Roughly when?
- What kind of record do you think it is?
- Where did you hear of it?

Staff then search for up to 20 minutes on the preparation half-day. There are three possible results:

- **Found.** The items go onto the slip and into the condition check.
- **Narrowed.** Staff call back with candidates and let the researcher choose.
- **Not found.** The researcher is offered a finding session, which is a booked desk with the printed catalog, indexes and open-shelf reference works, plus ten minutes of staff help at the start.

The 20-minute cap matters. Without it, description-only requests will absorb the preparation half-day.

### Walk-ins

Walk-ins continue to be welcome, but the offer changes. If a desk is free, the visitor may use it with finding aids and open-shelf material. Items from the store are not retrieved the same day, because they have not been checked. Staff complete a request slip and book a return visit before the visitor leaves.

A booked desk is held for 30 minutes after the session starts, then released to walk-ins.

### School groups

Groups book by telephone at least three weeks ahead and take the whole room for the weekly group session. The teacher states the topic, and staff select robust items or copies that have already been checked, so no pupil handles anything fragile. The teacher receives a one-page sheet on handling rules, group size and the lack of Wi-Fi.

### The magnifier

The slip records who needs the magnifier. Where possible, staff avoid booking two magnifier users into the same session. Where they cannot, both researchers are told in advance that it will be shared in 30-minute turns.

### What every researcher is told at confirmation

- The session time, and that the desk is held for 30 minutes.
- There is no public Wi-Fi, so any family trees, notes or references kept online should be brought on paper or downloaded beforehand.
- The handling rules and the photography decision.
- How to cancel, with the telephone number.

### If the staff member is absent

The room closes. Whoever opens the building telephones that day's researchers from the diary, and those researchers get first choice of the next available sessions. Each closure is recorded on the tally sheet, because the pilot needs to show how fragile a one-person service is.

## A difficult journey

This journey combines the hardest conditions: no internet use, no reference, a shared magnifier and an item that turns out to be unusable.

**The researcher.** A family historian in their late seventies with reduced eyesight. They do not use a computer. Their grandfather worked at a local tannery in the 1920s, and they have heard the archive holds "the wage books and a photograph of the men."

| Stage | What happens | Where it could fail | What the design does |
|---|---|---|---|
| First contact | They telephone at 11:00 on a Wednesday and reach the answerphone. | They give up, or leave no number. | The message states the staffed hour and promises a call back within two working days. |
| Call back | Staff ring at 4:15 the same day and use the five prompts. | Staff ask for a reference the caller cannot give. | The slip accepts a description. A desk is booked for the following Thursday and the magnifier need is recorded. |
| Search | On the preparation half-day, staff find a wage book for 1924–27 and a workforce photograph. | The search overruns. | The 20-minute cap applies; both items were found within it. |
| Condition check | The photograph is ready. The wage book has a detached spine and active mould. | The researcher travels in and finds out at the desk. | Staff telephone two working days ahead with the outcome and the options. |
| Options | Staff offer the photograph, a later volume in sound condition, and a staff-made transcript of the pages for the grandfather's surname. | Being told "not available" feels like a refusal. | The call starts with what can be seen, then explains what cannot. The researcher chooses to come. |
| The visit | The other desk is booked by someone who also needs the magnifier. | Two people wait on one tool. | Both were told in advance and take 30-minute turns. Staff start the researcher on the transcript, which needs no magnification. |
| Leaving | The researcher wants to return to the 1924 entries when the volume is repaired. | The interest is lost. | Staff note it on the slip and file it in a "contact when available" folder at the back of the diary. |

The journey shows where the pilot is most exposed: the call back, the search cap and the timing of the condition call. Those are the three points to watch.

## Running the pilot

**Before week 1**

- Rule up the diary with session pages for ten weeks.
- Print request slips and tally sheets.
- Record the answerphone message and add the sentence to the web form.
- Put a notice at the door and counter explaining the change, with the telephone number in large type.
- Walk the difficult journey through as a rehearsal with the front-desk team.

**Weeks 1–10**

Staff complete the tally sheet at the end of each public day; it should take five minutes. Front-desk staff also keep a notebook of anything that did not fit the rules, and what they did instead.

**Week 5**

The director and front-desk team hold a one-hour review. They change at most two rules, so the second half of the pilot can still be compared with the first.

**Week 10**

The team decides whether to continue, adjust or revert.

## What the pilot should teach

| Question | What to record | What it would mean |
|---|---|---|
| Is capacity right? | Desk-sessions booked, used, empty and refused for lack of space | Frequent refusals suggest more sessions; many empty desks suggest fewer or shorter ones |
| Who is using which route? | Telephone, web form or in person, by type of researcher | A fall in telephone and in-person use would suggest the service has become harder for people who cannot use forms |
| Does the staffed telephone hour work? | Answerphone messages, and the time taken to call back | Many missed calls mean the hour is at the wrong time or too short |
| What do description-only requests cost? | Number, minutes spent, and whether found, narrowed or not found | Whether the 20-minute cap holds, and whether finding sessions are worth offering |
| How often does condition change the visit? | Outcomes per item, and whether the researcher was told two days ahead | A high share of "not available" points to a need for copies of the most-requested fragile items |
| Is five days' notice right? | Days between request and visit, and any confirmations made late | Whether the lead time can shorten or must lengthen |
| What happens to walk-ins? | Number, whether seated, and whether they returned for the booked visit | Whether same-day visitors are being lost |
| Is one magnifier enough? | Sessions with two magnifier users, and any complaints | Whether a second magnifier is justified |
| Do group sessions work? | Groups booked, group size, preparation time and teacher comments | Whether one group session a week is too many or too few |
| Can one person sustain it? | Preparation time used against time allowed, and closures | Whether the opening pattern is realistic |

Two further questions need judgment as well as counts. First, staff should ask each researcher on leaving, "Did you see what you came to see?" and record yes, partly or no. Second, the team should discuss at week 5 and week 10 who has stopped coming, using the notebook and their own knowledge of regular visitors.

## Deciding at week 10

The service should continue if:

- most researchers saw what they came to see;
- nobody arrived to find an item unusable without warning;
- telephone and in-person requests held up alongside the web form;
- preparation fitted within the protected half-day.

If one of these fails, the tally sheet will show which rule to change. If preparation regularly overruns, the first change should be to reduce desk-sessions, since the two-step confirmation is what keeps the promise to researchers honest.

# Reservable study room: 10-week pilot proposal

## Decision and service promise

Approve a 10-week pilot with one appointment book, two reservable desks and a telephone, paper or web route into the same queue. Offer appointments for a defined period of study, with staff checking the requested material before confirming what the researcher can see. Keep a walk-in route for people who come to the archive to ask a first question. A useful outcome for a walk-in may be a seat that day, a later appointment, or help identifying which records to request.

The service promise should appear on the web form, the paper slip and the notice at the entrance. Use the same wording on the telephone.

> Tell us what you hope to find. A catalogue reference helps if you have one. We’ll agree how and when you’ll hear from us. We’ll confirm your desk and tell you which material we’ve checked for use. If we can’t offer the original, we’ll discuss your options before you travel.

The pilot should establish how much supported research one staff member can sustain, how reliably researchers can plan a worthwhile visit, and who still finds it difficult to get a place.

## Capacity and booking rules

Start with two 75-minute sessions on each of two existing opening days per week. The director should choose the days and publish the actual times before launch. Leave at least 30 minutes between sessions for returning material, resetting desks and recording follow-up. Set aside a further 45 minutes on each pilot day for calls, identification and condition checks. These are starting allowances to test against actual work. If preparation consistently overruns, reduce the number of appointments offered.

Each session has two desk places. Offer one in advance and keep one for short-notice demand until the preceding opening day. On that day, offer the second place to the earliest waiting researcher whose material is ready and who can attend. If still free, it can serve a same-day caller or walk-in with suitable material ready. Record which route uses the place. People using paper or telephone have the same access to advance and short-notice places as web users.

Book the magnifier by session alongside the desk. Ask whether it is essential and whether the researcher would welcome another time if it is taken. Where two people need it throughout, offer separate sessions. Keep the second desk available for a researcher who can use it independently. One member of staff must be able to supervise both desks. Book a session exclusively when a class visit or sustained staff assistance requires it, and record why the second desk was held.

A teacher should discuss numbers, ages, the research question and adult supervision by telephone or in person. Offer an exclusive session for a teacher and a small delegation that fits the room’s approved occupancy and two work surfaces. A larger class can work from a reproduction at school, if one is available and may be shared, or arrange separate small visits with an adult accompanying each group. Agree the arrangement before the school commits to travel.

## From enquiry to confirmation

**Receive the request.** Use one numbered paper slip per enquiry. Staff complete it with telephone callers and walk-ins and transcribe existing web submissions during the preparation period. Enter the original arrival date and time so a later transcription preserves the caller’s or sender’s place. Ask for a name, research question, any reference or identifying detail, preferred times, number attending, equipment or assistance needed, and a workable means of contact. Ask only for details needed to arrange the visit. Someone without a telephone or email address can take the request number and agree a time to call in for the answer.

**Identify the material.** About one request in five arrives without a catalogue reference. Ask what the person already knows and which fact they hope the records might establish. A street name, approximate year or former spelling may narrow the search. Allow an initial ten-minute search during preparation time. Record a likely reference and the reason it looks relevant, or one focused question for the researcher. If more work is needed, agree a further update or offer a short finding-aid consultation. Describe that appointment as a consultation so the person knows what the journey will buy them.

**Record a provisional hold.** Keep the staff appointment book as the single record of desk and magnifier availability. Enter the request number beside each resource held, mark the hold *provisional*, and agree an update by the end of the next pilot opening day. Tell the researcher whether this is a hold on a particular time or simply a request awaiting a suitable slot. If a visitor has a long journey or needs transport booked ahead, agree a decision deadline that works for them. A hold reserves capacity while staff investigate. It gives no assurance about the original.

**Check and confirm.** Before offering an original, retrieve it in a preparation period and check it under the archive’s existing handling procedures. Record the reference, check date, decision and any supports or limits on use. Uncertain condition goes to the director or the archive’s usual collections adviser, with access deferred pending a decision. If several items were requested, name each one cleared for use and explain what remains pending. Offer any suitable copy, related item or later date. Let the researcher decide whether the proposed visit is worthwhile.

Record the agreed time, desk, equipment, material and contact outcome. Mark the booking *confirmed* once the researcher accepts. Give directions, arrival instructions, the end time, and the telephone number for changes. Mention the lack of public Wi-Fi so visitors can bring downloaded notes or a paper list. If staff cannot reach someone, keep the hold until the deadline agreed at intake. Release the resources at that point, record the contact attempt and keep the research enquiry open for follow-up.

## At the front desk

Prepare checked material, supports, any booked magnifier and a paper call slip before the session. On arrival, match the visitor to the request number or name, show them where to put belongings, explain handling requirements and agree which item to start with. Bring out one unit at a time. Keep the appointment book and contact slips out of public view. For an unexpected visitor, check that supervision, a desk and appropriate material are all available before offering immediate study. During a supervised session, take a brief enquiry or agree a callback. Undertake retrieval when the room can be safely left.

Hold a confirmed place for 15 minutes after the start unless the visitor has called to agree otherwise. Publish this rule with the confirmation. After that, staff may offer the remaining time to someone already waiting with material ready. A late arrival can use any remaining capacity or rebook. If the sole staff member is absent, the director should arrange closure notices and use agreed contact routes to reach booked visitors as soon as possible. Give displaced visitors first choice of suitable replacement sessions.

At the end, check the material back in, record what was actually consulted, and offer a paper note of references and any next step. Ask one brief question before the visitor leaves: “What, if anything, made this visit hard to arrange or use?” Record the answer in their words if they agree. A person who declines an offered visit can answer the same question by telephone or on paper. Their experience matters even when no desk was occupied.

## A difficult journey to test

A family historian walks in on Tuesday with a former street name and an approximate year. She cannot use the web form, needs the magnifier and must arrange a lift. Both desks are occupied. The staff member takes a short paper enquiry within sight of the desks, asks what she wants to establish, and learns that she is trying to place her grandmother at a particular address. They agree a Thursday morning call before she books transport. She leaves with the request number, the time of the call and no expectation that a ledger has been found.

During preparation, staff identify a rate book covering the street. Its binding raises a handling concern, so they defer access. A checked street directory covers the same year, but lists named householders and may omit her grandmother. Thursday’s first available desk overlaps another researcher’s magnifier booking. At the agreed call, staff explain both constraints and the directory’s limits. They offer a later session with the directory and magnifier together, or a further update about the rate book. She chooses the directory. Staff read back the date and time and record her acceptance.

At the visit, the entry gives a different surname at the address. Staff help her record the citation and the limits of that evidence. She leaves with a specific next enquiry and chooses whether to receive an update about the ledger. A successful visit here is one she could judge worth making, with the equipment she needed. The pilot team should examine whether the promised call happened, how much identification time was needed, and whether the directory’s limitations were clear before she arranged the lift.

## Running the pilot and deciding what to keep

**Week 1.** The director selects sessions, sets preparation time and names a contact for uncertain condition decisions. Front-desk staff prepare the book, slips, entrance notice and telephone wording. Put the service promise beside the existing web form or in its acknowledgement. Rehearse the family-history journey and a school request against the same appointment page, then open bookings.

**Weeks 2–4.** Run the published sessions. Record requests by channel, missing references, promised and actual update dates, preparation minutes, condition decisions, magnifier conflicts and visit outcomes. Count people turned away or unable to accept the dates offered. Use request numbers on the tally sheet and keep contact details on the separate slips under the archive’s existing retention practice.

**Week 5.** Review the tally with the director. Trace one request from each channel, including one that did not become a visit. Check whether late transcription, missed calls or short-notice release rules disadvantaged anyone. Make one documented adjustment where possible, such as moving the callback period or changing when the second desk is released. Tell staff and visitors when it takes effect.

**Weeks 6–9.** Run the revised arrangement. Each week compare occupied desk places with places offered, alongside time spent preparing and reasons for unused places. Record exclusive sessions separately so a school visit or assisted visit is counted accurately. Check whether appointments displaced walk-in help or pushed preparation beyond paid time.

**Week 10.** Decide whether to retain, revise or reduce the service. Use two proposed benchmarks: at least 90% of promised updates delivered on time, and every original offered for use backed by a recorded condition check. Report counts alongside percentages because the pilot is small. Compare waiting times and unfulfilled requests across channels and between requests with and without references. Review comments from visitors and people who declined. Retain the schedule if preparation fits available hours and researchers can obtain a usable appointment through all three routes. Where the evidence falls short, identify the specific constraint, assign an owner and set a review date before making the revised schedule permanent.

# Reservable study room pilot

## Decision for the director

Run a 10-week pilot with two reservable desks, one shared magnifier and one staff member on duty. Accept requests by telephone, on paper at the front desk and through the existing web form. Use one paper booking ledger for all three channels. Give visitors a confirmed time to use the room and a separate update on whether their requested material is ready. This distinction matters when a researcher has yet to identify an item or when staff must check its condition.

The pilot should answer three questions. Can visitors secure a useful visit regardless of how they contact the archive? Can one staff member prepare material and supervise two desks within the time available? Does reserving ahead reduce wasted trips, especially for people whose requests arrive without a catalog reference? Those requests currently account for about one in five, so identifying material needs a regular place in the schedule.

## Room hours and capacity

Start with two study-room blocks a week, scheduled around the archive’s existing duties. In each block, offer two 60-minute sessions with a 15-minute reset between them. This gives a maximum of eight desk bookings per week before group bookings or staff absences. Schedule a separate 45-minute preparation period for each block. Put those preparation periods on the staff calendar alongside the public sessions. If preparation repeatedly spills over, reduce the number of desks released or sessions offered before adding hours.

Use one desk per researcher or per pair working together if the room can accommodate the pair safely. Ask about accompanying adults, support people and students at intake. Agree on a group size the room and staff member can handle before confirming a school visit. Offer schools an exclusive room session, with the teacher supervising students and only the agreed number working at the desks. Where a class is too large, offer a small delegation or discuss rotations if the school can supervise students outside the room and the site has space. Each exclusive session uses both desk slots.

Book the magnifier in the same ledger as the desks. Ask about it when taking a request and agree on a time window if two visitors need it. If someone needs it throughout their visit, reserve it for their full session and offer the other visitor a different time if necessary. Tell visitors at confirmation that there is no public Wi-Fi. Suggest saving references, notes or instructions to their device beforehand or bringing them on paper.

## From request to confirmation

**Take the same information through each channel.** Ask for the visitor’s name, a reliable way to contact them, preferred times, party size, any practical access needs, and what they want to see or learn. Record a catalog reference if they have one. If they do not, ask for two or three clues, such as a place, date range, name, address or type of record. Capture the research question in the visitor’s own words. For telephone and counter requests, staff complete the intake with the visitor. Use the fields already available on the web form, with any extra information collected during follow-up. Post the telephone number and walk-in booking option wherever the web form is advertised.

**Use one ledger to allocate time.** Give each request a number and record its arrival date and channel. Enter web requests during a scheduled daily check on staffed days. Allocate available times in request order among visitors whose times and room needs fit. Keep names and contact details in a staff-only section. In the schedule, use request numbers and record desk, time, magnifier allocation and any setup needed. When offering a time, give a reply deadline, usually the end of the next staffed day. Release an unanswered hold after that deadline and record the outcome. Visitors who accept at the counter or by phone can be confirmed immediately.

**Set a clear expectation about materials.** Keep a room status and a material status for each request. The room can be requested, held, confirmed or closed. Each requested item can be awaiting identification, awaiting condition check, cleared or unavailable for use. A booking confirmation should state the time, arrival instructions, any equipment allocation and when staff will update the visitor about materials. Use plain language such as, “Your desk is reserved for Thursday at 10. We still need to check whether the volume can be handled. We’ll call by Wednesday afternoon so you can decide whether to travel.”

Aim to acknowledge requests by the end of the next staffed day. Offer dates that leave a preparation period before the visit. Agree on a material decision deadline, normally the staffed day before the visit and earlier when visitors need time to arrange travel or transport. Ask whether a message may be left and what it may include. For visitors who cannot reliably receive calls, agree on a time for them to call back or collect an update in person. A missed call leaves the material status unresolved for the visitor.

## Preparation and running the room

During preparation, start with the requests whose visitors need a decision soonest. For a request without a reference, spend up to 15 minutes on an initial search using the clues provided. If it remains unresolved, record what was searched and offer a focused follow-up. Ask for a missing detail, propose an identified source that addresses the question, or agree on a visit focused on finding aids. Use the pilot to see whether the initial search allowance is sufficient.

Pull candidate material during preparation and check condition and any handling restrictions under the archive’s existing procedures. Record the item and the decision. Where an item is unsuitable or its condition remains uncertain, keep it off the desk and explain what can be offered instead. A cleared duplicate, existing surrogate, related record or finding aid may make the visit worthwhile. Describe what the substitute covers so the visitor can decide whether to keep, reschedule or cancel their booking. If staff miss the agreed update deadline, contact the visitor as soon as possible with the current status and available choices.

Before opening, set out cleared items and any necessary supports, check the magnifier and review the two bookings. At arrival, confirm the booking and explain handling, note-taking and any photography rules that apply. Issue and account for material using the archive’s existing procedures. Keep both desks within sight. Schedule retrieval and condition checks outside supervised sessions. If a visitor requests another item during a session, record it for a later check. If a front-desk duty requires staff to leave the room, pause handling and secure the material first. Close the block and contact booked visitors if the sole staff member is unavailable.

Ask visitors to cancel by phone, at the counter or through any reply channel already available to them. Offer released slots to people who have agreed to short-notice contact, allowing time for preparation. Ask late arrivals to call if they can. After 15 minutes without contact, staff may release the desk if someone can use it and suitable material is ready. A late arrival can use the remaining time if the desk is still free. Walk-ins can request a future visit or take a free desk when staff can supervise and there is suitable cleared material. Post this arrangement at the entrance.

## A difficult visit

A family historian calls from a landline. She cannot use the web form, travels in on a bus that runs twice a day and needs the magnifier to read small print. She wants to find the shop her grandmother ran, but knows only the surname, a street and an approximate decade.

Staff take the request by phone and ask for a spelling variant and the nearest cross street. They offer a session that fits the bus and reserve the magnifier for the full hour. The caller has no voicemail, so they agree she will ring the day before her visit at a time when staff can give her an answer. Staff explain that the desk is reserved while they identify and check the records.

The likely street directory turns out to have loose pages and cannot be issued. Staff find a cleared directory from two years later and a street index. On the agreed call, they explain the date difference and what each source can tell her. She decides to come because the later directory may establish the address. At check-in, the records and magnifier are ready. She finds a plausible address, and staff record the next search she wants to pursue.

If she misses the agreed call, staff keep the desk reserved under the terms already agreed and make one outbound attempt if she has agreed to receive it. If she travels without reaching staff, the team can explain the condition decision and offer the prepared alternatives. Record whether she received the update before travelling, whether the substitute served her purpose and how much staff time the search took. A kept appointment alone would miss the cost of a wasted bus trip or a substitute that answered the wrong question.

## Ten-week learning plan

In week 1, set up the ledger, post the booking routes and hours, and rehearse three cases before the first session begins. Use a request without a reference, an item that fails its condition check, and two researchers who need the magnifier at the same time. The director should agree with staff on room occupancy and which existing duties can be deferred during supervised sessions. In weeks 2–4, run the published schedule and review the ledger for 15 minutes each week. In week 5, adjust the largest recurring bottleneck, such as the timing of preparation or the way staff ask for identifying clues. Record the change and its date. Continue through week 9 and use week 10 to review the evidence and decide what to retain.

Use simple ticks and counts in the ledger. Track requests by channel, those arriving without a reference, confirmed and completed visits, cancellations, no-shows and people who could not find a suitable time. For materials, record whether staff gave the update by the agreed deadline, whether the original item or an alternative was used, and whether availability prevented the visit. Total the minutes spent on intake, identification, preparation and supervision each week. Note when a session disrupted another duty or when two bookings competed for the magnifier. Keep tally sheets free of names and handle the booking ledger under the archive’s existing records procedures.

At checkout, ask, “Did you make progress on what you came to find?” and “What made booking or visiting difficult?” Where practical, ask people who cancel or decline an offered slot what got in the way. Compare counts and examples across channels and between requests with and without references. A small pilot will yield clues about where the service breaks down. For example, timely acknowledgments alongside late material updates would point to preparation capacity. Low repeat demand after school visits could warrant asking teachers about scheduling, group size or whether the sources fit the lesson.

At week 10, retain the model if visitors can book through all three channels, staff generally meet the material update deadlines, and sessions fit alongside other duties. Adjust hours, desk capacity or preparation time if the ledger shows a recurring constraint. Pause or reduce service if staff cannot supervise the room or complete condition checks reliably. The director’s decision should use both the visits delivered and the requests the archive could not serve, with attention to who bore the cost when a booking or material decision fell through.
